subject: Behavioral Economics
title: The Consistency Trap
description: A 60-second lesson on The Consistency Trap.

hook.text: A CEO publicly declared a strategy brilliant. Six months later, data proved it wrong. She doubled down anyway.

buildup.text: Once we commit publicly, changing course feels like admitting failure. Consistency becomes a cage.

discovery.text: Cialdini showed that public commitments create internal pressure to stay consistent, even against new evidence.

twist.text: Wise leaders reframe changing direction as learning, not failure. Flexibility is strength, not weakness.

climax.text: When defending a past position, ask: am I protecting the idea or my ego? The answer changes everything.

punchline.text: Foolish consistency is the mind's most expensive lock.

quiz.question: Why is public commitment a trap?
options: Others will enforce the commitment legally
It creates internal pressure to stay consistent even against new evidence
Public commitments always lead to better outcomes

details.summary: The consistency trap drives people to maintain positions, commitments, and beliefs even when new evidence suggests they should change course. Once you publicly commit to a position, the desire to appear consistent overrides the rationality of updating your view.
details.whyItMatters: The consistency trap makes leaders, politicians, and organizations persist with failing strategies because reversing course looks like weakness or flip-flopping. The social cost of appearing inconsistent can exceed the actual cost of a poor decision.
takeaways: Public commitments create pressure to maintain positions regardless of evidence
Changing your mind based on new evidence is rational but socially costly
Cultures that reward consistency over accuracy create decision traps

faq.question: Why do people value consistency over being correct?
faq.answer: Inconsistency signals unreliability in social contexts. Changing positions is interpreted as weakness or confusion rather than learning. The social penalty for appearing inconsistent often exceeds the private benefit of being right.

faq.question: How can organizations reward evidence-based updating?
faq.answer: Celebrate instances of leaders changing their minds based on evidence. Normalize update language like 'based on new information, I now believe.' Separate the quality of the initial judgment from the quality of the updating process.
